United States Hurricane Return Periods

How often, on average, a hurricane can be expected to strike each U.S. coastal county — based on every recorded storm in the HURDAT2 database. Click any county for its full strike history; hover for a quick read.
MICHAEL FERRAGAMO
1851–2026

What is a Return Period?

It is the average length of time a location goes between storm strikes. In this case, a U.S. coastal county. A 30 nautical mile radius is implemented around each county to account for strikes — all of which is calculated from the full HURDAT2 record (1851–2025). A shorter return period means a county has historically been struck more often.

Data across the TROPICAL CYCLONE DATABASE is powered by the Atlantic Hurricane Database (HURDAT2, 1851–2025) for all landfall positions, wind, and pressure. The database was also utilized to recover landfalls HURDAT2 didn't flag. A landfall counts if a storm’s center crosses a coastline at tropical storm strength or above. This website is built as a reference and educational tool, so as always, confirm figures/decisions against the National Hurricane Center’s official reports.
